opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was how much the small details matter, and how easy it is to fool yourself with a single number.

GPQA is a great benchmark because the questions are genuinely hard. They were written by domain experts in biology, physics, and chemistry, and they're designed so that skilled non-experts with web access still struggle. So when a model does well, it feels meaningful. But once you start reporting results, you realize that the headline score depends heavily on choices that rarely make it into the chart: which subset you use, whether it's zero-shot or few-shot, whether you allow chain-of-thought, how you parse the final answer, how many samples you average over, and so on.

The dataset is also relatively small, especially the harder subsets, so variance is real. A couple of points of difference between two models might just be noise. Running it multiple times and reporting confidence intervals, or at least being transparent about the setup, became really important to me. Otherwise you get people comparing numbers across labs that were never measured the same way.

The other thing it taught me is that evals are a product in themselves. How you frame a result shapes how people understand the model's capabilities. If you say a model is at "expert level" on GPQA, people hear "this model is a PhD scientist," and that's not quite what the benchmark measures. It measures performance on a particular format of multiple-choice questions. That's useful signal, but it's not the same as doing research, designing experiments, or knowing when you're wrong.

So my takeaway was: be rigorous about methodology, be humble about what a number means, and pair benchmarks with qualitative evaluation, actually looking at the model's reasoning, talking to domain experts, and seeing how it behaves on open-ended tasks. Benchmarks saturate quickly, and the most interesting questions about a model usually live in the places the benchmark doesn't cover.

r001.rationale: It says GPQA’s small dataset makes variance real and that a few points of difference may be noise.

r002.rationale: It says comparisons across labs can be misleading when setups differ, but does not identify evaluation numbers in the model card as not directly comparable to one another.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So GPQA is this graduate-level science benchmark, and the thing that stuck with me is that the number you report is really a bundle of decisions, not a single fact about the model.

The first lesson was about variance. GPQA Diamond is only a couple hundred questions, so a single run can swing a few points just from sampling noise. If you report one number with no error bars, you are basically reporting a dice roll with extra steps. We got into the habit of running multiple seeds and showing the spread, and once you do that, a lot of the "we beat the previous model by two points" claims start looking a lot less meaningful.

The second thing was prompting and scaffolding. Zero-shot, few-shot, chain of thought, majority voting over 32 samples, with or without a system prompt. Each one gives you a different number, and all of them are "GPQA." So when you compare against someone else's headline score, you often are not comparing the same thing. I became pretty insistent on writing down the exact setup, because otherwise the comparison is just marketing.

Then there was the contamination question. Those questions are on the internet. The experts who wrote them had to make them hard for people with web access, but models trained after the dataset was published might have seen them. You cannot fully rule that out, so we started treating high scores as a reason to look harder, not as a reason to celebrate.

And honestly the deepest lesson was about what the benchmark is for. GPQA was designed to test whether a model can answer questions that even skilled non-experts cannot answer with Google. That is a specific capability. It tells you something about reasoning on hard, well-posed questions. It tells you very little about whether the model will be useful to an actual chemist sitting in a lab with a messy, underspecified problem. I think a lot of people, including me early on, slid from "the model does well on GPQA" to "the model is good at science," and those are not the same statement.

So the way I think about it now is that benchmarks are instruments. You need to know their resolution, their failure modes, and what they are actually measuring. The number is the beginning of the evaluation, not the end of it. The real work is the qualitative stuff: reading transcripts, looking at where it fails, and asking whether the failures are the kind that matter for the thing you care about.

r001.rationale: It describes GPQA Diamond as small and says scores can swing by a few points from sampling noise, recommending multiple seeds and showing the spread.

r002.rationale: It explains that different prompts and scaffolding produce different GPQA scores and that comparing headline scores often means comparing different setups.

astra-6.text:
The biggest lesson was that a benchmark score needs a lot of context. You can report a number that looks very precise, but what exactly was the setup? How did you prompt the model? How much did the result vary between runs? Were you comparing models under the same conditions?

With something like GPQA, it’s tempting to turn a strong score into a much broader claim about scientific reasoning. But answering a difficult multiple-choice question is only one slice of that capability. It doesn’t automatically tell you whether the model can do research or reliably help a scientist.

So I think reporting is part of evaluation itself. You need to communicate what the result supports, where the uncertainty is, and what it leaves unanswered. The number should be the start of the conversation.

r001.rationale: The response asks how much results vary between runs but does not state that GPQA is a high-variance evaluation.

r002.rationale: It raises whether models were compared under the same conditions, but does not state that the model-card evaluation numbers are not directly comparable.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest lesson is that a benchmark score needs context. With something like GPQA, you want to know how the questions were presented, whether the model could use tools, how much time or computation it had, and how much the result varies across runs. Those details can change what a comparison actually means.

So I’d treat the score as one piece of evidence. It tells you something about performance on a particular set of difficult questions, but it doesn’t automatically tell you how useful or reliable the model will be in practice. Looking at the failures—and being clear about the evaluation setup—is just as important as reporting the number.

r001.rationale: The response says results can vary across runs, but does not identify GPQA itself as a high-variance evaluation.
